text: RBAC so far has been about human users. But Northbridge also has a catalog-sync Pod that calls the Kubernetes API directly, and it needs its own identity to authenticate with — separate from any person. That identity is a ServiceAccount.

Every Pod already has one, whether anyone configured it or not. Skip the field and Kubernetes assigns the default ServiceAccount of that namespace automatically. It usually has no permissions bound to it, so it's harmless — but it's still an identity, and a Pod that genuinely needs API access deserves its own dedicated account instead of sharing default with everything else.

Creating one looks just like creating a user identity. A RoleBinding's subjects entry uses kind: ServiceAccount instead of kind: User, naming it and its namespace — everything else about binding a Role works exactly the same as the last lesson.

The Pod opts in with serviceAccountName. Kubernetes mounts that ServiceAccount's token into the container, the application presents it to the API server, and the server checks it against whatever RBAC rules are actually bound to catalog-sync — in this case, just get and list on ConfigMaps.

Most Pods never touch the API at all — a checkout Pod serving HTTP traffic has no reason to hold a token. Setting automountServiceAccountToken to false stops that token from being mounted where it isn't needed, shrinking what an attacker could reuse if the Pod were ever compromised.
Identity answers who's making the request. Next up, lesson twenty-seven: Pod Security, which locks down what a container is allowed to do once it's actually running.
